pending_items.title: Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
pending_items.content:
Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.

Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.

Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.

Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.

Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.

“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here,” Badilla continued without elaborating. “Our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system.”

While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.

On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.

Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the university has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.

As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide , for which she received numerous threats , Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.

Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.

She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.

In her July 2025 report , she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google , alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.

On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”

Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.

After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.

Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.

The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.

In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.

The most significant escalation came in July 2025, when the Trump administration imposed sanctions against Albanese, accusing her of pursuing a campaign of political and economic warfare against Israel and the United States.

The measures included restrictions on Albanese entering the US, blocking her property and financial interests subject to US jurisdiction and prohibiting US nationals from engaging in transactions with her, effectively isolating her from much of the US financial system.

The US decision was roundly condemned by the UN and various rights groups.

A committee of the UN’s Human Rights Council characterised it as just one aspect of the “continued assault of the current US administration on the entire UN system and its core values of human rights, justice, accountability and the rule of law”. Rights groups, including Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International, also criticised the decision, with the latter slamming the US measures as a “disgraceful affront to international justice”.

pending_items.title: As Spain’s right eyes power, what would change for Israel, Morocco and Algeria?
pending_items.content:
“The Israeli government has all our support, affection and understanding,” Santiago Abascal, leader of Spain’s far-right Vox party, said during a trip to Israel in December 2023.

While Abascal visited Israel in a show of support and to seek political backing from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli forces had killed more than 16,248 Palestinians in Gaza, according to figures cited by the UN humanitarian office, OCHA. About 70 percent were women and children.

Spain votes on Sunday, with polls predicting that Vox will almost double its parliamentary representation from 33 seats to 61.

That would help the centre-right People’s Party (PP), which polls project will win 129 seats, assemble a coalition comfortably above the 176-seat majority needed to unseat Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s centre-left government.

The election could also change Spain’s foreign policy, including its relationship with US President Donald Trump, its tense relations with Morocco and its deteriorating ties with Israel over the genocide in Gaza and ongoing apartheid policies in the occupied West Bank.

Domestic issues, including the cost of living, affordable housing, wages and immigration, have dominated the campaign since Sanchez called the snap election on 5 October.

Those concerns have driven support for Vox and the PP more than any shift in public attitudes towards foreign policy.

According to a June survey by Pew Research Center, around 66 percent of Spaniards on the self-identified political right viewed Israel unfavourably, compared with 79 percent in the centre and 96 percent on the left.

“The historical and traditional stance held by all Spanish governments [towards Palestine] since the transition to democracy in the 1970s enjoyed a broad consensus across the political spectrum - among conservatives, socialists, left-wing parties, and nationalists alike - and commanded widespread public support,” said Isaiah Barrenada Bajo, an international relations professor at Complutense University of Madrid.

Under former PP prime minister Jose Maria Aznar, who governed Spain from 1996 to 2004 and took the country into the Iraq war, “a shift occurred toward a neoconservative, more Atlanticist, and pro-Israel orientation,” Barrenada told Middle East Eye.

“This perspective has persisted within one faction of the PP to this day; it is especially prominent within the far-right party Vox - considered the most pro-Israel party in the European Parliament - upon which the PP might well depend to secure a governing majority,” he added.

Israel’s diaspora affairs minister, Amichai Chikli, called Abascal “a personal friend” and “one of Israel’s greatest supporters in Europe” during a podcast in April this year.

Abascal has also promised to reverse Spain’s recognition of a Palestinian state.

Spain formally recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024, alongside Ireland and Norway. Sanchez announced the decision in parliament six days earlier, summing up his reasons in three words: “Peace, justice and coherence.”

Sanchez has arguably been one of Europe’s strongest voices in demanding accountability for Israel’s crimes in Palestine.

Alongside recognising the genocide in Gaza, Sanchez said the bombing campaign against the besieged strip would become “one of the darkest episodes of this century”. He said he wanted Spaniards to be able to say they had stood “on the right side of history”.

Spain has also supported South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.

“The recognition of the State of Palestine - though long overdue, having been demanded by parliament and civil society for over a decade - was welcomed by the majority of the population, regardless of whether they supported the current government or identified with the opposition,” Barrenada said.

'Historically, the Spanish right has been much firmer in responding to Morocco’s blackmail, hostility and pressure than the Socialist Party'

Relations with Israel, meanwhile, have hit rock bottom since 2023. Both countries have withdrawn their ambassadors. Spain has sanctioned some Israeli settlers, banned imports from Israeli colonial outposts in the West Bank, introduced an arms embargo and condemned Trump’s plan to ethnically cleanse Gaza.

When more than 60,000 Moroccan migrants crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta in August, many in Spain blamed Rabat and Tel Aviv for orchestrating the crisis. Israeli leaders relished the crisis, during which more than 100 Moroccans drowned attempting the dangerous crossing.

In September, Aznar, a staunch supporter of Israel, linked the Ceuta crisis to Spain’s deteriorating relationship with Israel. He suggested it resulted from "[alienating] the friendship of relevant allies, those allies one should be able to count on in crises". He called for the "normalisation of diplomatic relations with Israel as soon as possible".

The migration crisis emboldened the Spanish far right, which sought to portray Sanchez as weak on border security and unwilling to confront Morocco over its weaponisation of migrants.

“Historically, the Spanish right has been much firmer in responding to Morocco’s blackmail, hostility and pressure than the Socialist Party, which has consistently demonstrated an attitude of submission towards Rabat,” Taleb Alisalem, a Sahrawi writer and political analyst based in Madrid, told MEE.

“However, I personally do not believe that the People’s Party will go as far as reversing Pedro Sanchez’s decision to support Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara.”

Sanchez’s 2022 decision to back Morocco’s autonomy plan for Western Sahara proved controversial because it offers the territory limited self-rule under Moroccan sovereignty, while the Polisario Front seeks a referendum allowing the Sahrawi people to choose independence.

The move also triggered a rupture in relations with energy-rich Algeria .

“Could there be a rapprochement with Algeria? Certainly. Mainly because of energy interests. Algeria is a major gas producer with substantial reserves and supplies a significant proportion of the natural gas consumed in Spain. I believe a right-wing government would seek to rebuild and strengthen relations with Algiers,” Alisalem said.

“But Morocco also has considerable means of exerting pressure, extending far beyond its relationship with the Socialist Party. Rabat could also put pressure on the PP and even Vox, including through its close relationship with Israel.”

Latin America offers a recent precedent for how a change from a left-wing to a right-wing government can dramatically shift foreign policy towards Israel and the US.

In August, Colombia’s newly elected far-right government, led by Abelardo de la Espriella, recognised Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Syrian Golan Heights. It also announced plans to move its embassy to west Jerusalem.

Moussa Bourekba, a research fellow at the Barcelona Centre for International Affairs and author of Escalation within Continuity: Spain’s Foreign Policy towards Israel and Palestine after October 7th , told MEE that Spain was unlikely to undergo such a dramatic shift.

During an election debate on Thursday, PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo described events in Gaza as “a massacre” and “unacceptable”.

“Vox clearly has a sense of unconditional support to Israel,” Bourekba said, adding that “PP could not openly go against the move of recognition of Palestine, because that would mean going against what the Spaniards believe and think”.

“My argument here is that the very same way that leftist parties within the current coalition government led by Sanchez have been very influential in pushing him to raise the tone against Israel, to adopt sanctions, and to show solidarity with Palestine, we could expect Vox to act in a similar manner with PP, but in the opposite direction.”

pending_items.title: In Iran, child marriage risks complicated by war
pending_items.content:
For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.

The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly in 2025.

Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the impact of the conflict.

In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband . Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran, said the girl had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.

"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk ," Thompson told DW.

Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 between roughly March 2025 and March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.

The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.

Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.

But the latest figures largely predate the war , which began on February 28, 2026.

"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.

The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.

In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.

Thompson said that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government-backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Ottawa, Canada, described a similar risk.

When families cannot meet a girl's living costs and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her toward marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.

Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.

Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene on their behalf.

Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.

Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below the age of 18.

"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.

Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.

The concerns also extend to the online space. An investigation published by Human Rights Activists in Iran in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted, or whether the war increased them.

Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.

"Education alone is not enough," he said. Families also need the means to support their children.

Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.

According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.
